question: What did the medieval term “Raqs” mean?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dancing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• ‘Raqs’ is a Perso-Arabic term meaning dance/dancing, which entered Indian usage during the medieval (Delhi Sultanate–Mughal) period. (रक्स — नृत्य)

• Medieval Persian chronicles of the Sultanate and Mughal courts describe raqs (dance) alongside sama (spiritual music assembly) and naql (mimicry/storytelling).

• Sufi assemblies, especially of the Chishti order, used sama and ecstatic raqs as forms of devotion; Amir Khusrau is closely linked with this musical–dance culture.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Singing in medieval Persianate usage is ghina/naghma, and a singer is a gayak/qawwal.

• Chanting of hymns in Sufi practice is broadly zikr (dhikr) — repetition of God’s names.

• Ritual would be rasm/rivaj, not raqs.

NOTE

• Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, is credited in tradition with the qawwali, and with instruments/forms like the sitar and tabla (traditional attribution).

• Medieval music texts to remember: Man Kautuhal (Raja Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior) and Ragadarpan (Faqirullah, Aurangzeb’s reign).

question: बौद्ध स्थापत्यकला के स्मारकों में प्रार्थना कक्षों को ________ कहा जाता था।
solution_text:
The correct answer is चैत्य गृह (Chaitya griha).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In Buddhist architecture the prayer hall/assembly hall is the Chaitya griha; it is typically an apsidal hall with a stupa at the far end, a nave and side aisles separated by pillars. (चैत्य गृह — प्रार्थना गृह)

• Famous rock-cut chaityas: Karle (largest, Maharashtra), Bhaja, Bedsa, Ajanta caves 9, 10, 19, 26 and Ellora cave 10 (Vishvakarma).

• Chaityas usually have a horseshoe-shaped chaitya window (surya/gavaksha) over the entrance for light.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• विहार (Vihara) — the residence/monastery of monks, a square courtyard surrounded by cells.

• स्तूप (Stupa) — a hemispherical relic mound; e.g., Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati.

• पिश्तक (Pishtaq) — a tall arched gateway/portal, a feature of Indo-Islamic, not Buddhist, architecture.

NOTE

• Stupa parts: anda (dome), harmika (railing on top), chhatra (umbrella), medhi (drum), vedika (railing), toranas (gateways), pradakshina patha (circumambulatory path).

• The Sanchi Stupa was originally built by Ashoka and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1989).

question: Pankaj Advani is associated with which sports?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Billiards.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pankaj Advani (born 1985, Pune; based in Bengaluru) is India’s greatest cue sportsman, playing billiards and snooker. (बिलियर्ड्स — क्यू खेल)

• He has won more than 25 world titles and is the only player to have completed a ‘Grand Double’ — winning both the time format and point format of the World Billiards Championship in the same year (2005).

• Awards: Arjuna Award (2004), Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna (2005–06), Padma Shri (2009) and Padma Bhushan (2018).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Table Tennis — Indian names: Sharath Kamal, Manika Batra, Sathiyan Gnanasekaran.

• Chess — Viswanathan Anand (first Indian Grandmaster, 5-time World Champion), R. Praggnanandhaa, D. Gukesh.

• Golf — Jeev Milkha Singh, Anirban Lahiri, Aditi Ashok, Shubhankar Sharma.

NOTE

• Cue-sport terms: cue, baulk line, cannon, break, pot, century break.

• Billiards/snooker are governed internationally by the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA); in India by the Billiards and Snooker Federation of India (BSFI).

question: Which among the following books is an autobiography of Mithali Raj?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Unguarded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• ‘Unguarded’ is the autobiography of Mithali Raj, the former captain of the Indian women’s cricket team. (आत्मकथा)

• Mithali Raj (born 3 December 1982, Jodhpur) is the highest run-scorer in women’s international cricket and led India to the World Cup finals in 2005 and 2017.

• Awards: Arjuna Award (2003), Padma Shri (2015) and Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna (2021). The film ‘Shabaash Mithu’ (2022), starring Taapsee Pannu, is based on her life.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• All Round View — autobiography of the Pakistani all-rounder Imran Khan.

• No Holding Back — autobiography of the West Indian fast bowler Michael Holding.

• One More Over — autobiography of the Indian off-spinner Erapalli Prasanna.

NOTE

• Other cricket autobiographies/biographies: Playing It My Way (Sachin Tendulkar), A Century Is Not Enough (Sourav Ganguly), The Test of My Life (Yuvraj Singh), Straight from the Heart (Kapil Dev).

question: What is the tenure of a Rajya Sabha member?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Six years.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A member of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) is elected for a term of six years. (राज्य सभा — छह वर्ष)

• The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house — it is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every two years (Article 83(1)).

• Maximum strength is 250 (238 elected from States/UTs + 12 nominated by the President for art, literature, science and social service); present strength is 245.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Five years is the normal term of the Lok Sabha and of State Legislative Assemblies (Article 83(2), 172).

• Minimum age: 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha.

• The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64).

NOTE

• Rajya Sabha members are elected by the elected MLAs of States by proportional representation with a single transferable vote (open ballot).

• Exclusive powers of the Rajya Sabha: Article 249 (law on a State List subject in national interest) and Article 312 (creation of a new All-India Service).

question: Who established the Ramakrishna Mission?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Swami Vivekananda.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Ramakrishna Mission was founded on 1 May 1897 at Kolkata by Swami Vivekananda (born Narendranath Datta, 12 January 1863) in memory of his guru Ramakrishna Paramahansa. (रामकृष्ण मिशन)

• Its headquarters is at Belur Math, Howrah, West Bengal, established in 1899. Its motto is ‘Atmano mokshartham jagat hitaya cha’ — for one’s own salvation and for the welfare of the world.

• Vivekananda addressed the World’s Parliament of Religions at Chicago on 11 September 1893; his birthday is observed as National Youth Day.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Tarun Sagar — a Digambara Jain monk, known for his discourses ‘Kadve Pravachan’.

• Jambuvijaya — a Shvetambara Jain monk and scholar of Jain manuscripts.

• Gaur Gopal Das — a contemporary ISKCON monk and motivational speaker.

NOTE

• Socio-religious reform bodies: Brahmo Samaj – Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1828), Arya Samaj – Dayanand Saraswati (1875), Prarthana Samaj – Atmaram Pandurang (1867), Theosophical Society – Blavatsky & Olcott (1875).

• Vivekananda’s works: Raja Yoga, Karma Yoga, Jnana Yoga, Bhakti Yoga.

question: Which among the following is a famous festival of Maharashtra, India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gudi Padva.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Gudi Padva is the traditional New Year festival of Maharashtra (and the Konkan region), celebrated on Chaitra Shukla Pratipada, i.e., the first day of the Hindu lunisolar month of Chaitra (March–April). (गुड़ी पाडवा — नव वर्ष)

• A ‘gudi’ — a bamboo pole topped with a bright cloth, neem leaves, a garland and an inverted copper/silver pot — is hoisted at the doorway as a symbol of victory and prosperity.

• Other Maharashtrian festivals often asked: Ganesh Chaturthi, Nag Panchami, Ellora Ajanta Festival and Pola (bullock festival).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Ugadi — the New Year of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka (where it is also called Yugadi).

• Chhath Puja — a sun-worship festival of Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh, dedicated to Surya and Chhathi Maiya.

• Onam — the harvest festival of Kerala, associated with the legendary king Mahabali; features Vallamkali boat race and Pookalam.

NOTE

• New Year names by region: Baisakhi (Punjab), Bihu (Assam), Puthandu (Tamil Nadu), Vishu (Kerala), Navreh (Kashmir), Cheti Chand (Sindhi), Losar (Ladakh/Tibetan).

question: Fishes have ______ chambers of the heart.
solution_text:
The correct answer is two.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A fish heart has two chambers — one atrium (auricle) and one ventricle. (मछली — दो कक्षीय हृदय)

• Fish show single circulation: blood passes through the heart only once in one complete cycle — heart → gills (oxygenation) → body → heart.

• Only deoxygenated blood flows through a fish’s heart, so there is no mixing problem as in three-chambered hearts.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Three chambers — amphibians (frogs) and most reptiles: two atria and one ventricle, with some mixing of blood.

• Four chambers — birds, mammals and crocodiles: two atria and two ventricles, complete double circulation with no mixing.

• One chamber — not found in vertebrates; some invertebrates have a simple tubular or open circulatory system (e.g., cockroach).

NOTE

• The human heart weighs about 250–350 g and beats about 72 times per minute; the SA node is the natural pacemaker.

• Fish breathe through gills; the pericardium is the membrane covering the heart.

question: The summer months experience ______ in the northern part of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is falling air pressure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• During summer (March–May) intense heating of north-western India raises temperatures, the air expands and rises, and so the surface air pressure falls. (निम्न वायुदाब)

• By June an elongated low-pressure trough — the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) — develops over the Thar and Ganga plains; this monsoon trough pulls in moist south-west winds from the sea.

• This land–sea pressure difference is the classical explanation for the onset of the South-West Monsoon in early June.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Rising air pressure occurs in winter, when the land cools and a high-pressure area forms over north-western India, giving dry offshore north-east winds.

• Decreasing temperature is wrong — summer temperatures rise, often crossing 45°C in the north-west.

• Heavy rain belongs to the rainy season (mid-June to September), not to the hot-weather season.

NOTE

• Local summer winds/phenomena: Loo (hot dry wind of north India), Kalbaisakhi/Norwesters (West Bengal & Assam), Mango showers (Kerala & Karnataka), Blossom shower (coffee, Karnataka).

question: The kingdoms of Chola, Chera and Pandyas belong to which period in the ancient India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sangam Period.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas — called the ‘muvendar’ (three crowned kings) — ruled south India during the Sangam Age, roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE. (संगम काल)

• The Sangam was an assembly of Tamil poets held under the patronage of the Pandya kings of Madurai; three Sangams are traditionally mentioned.

• Capitals and emblems: Chera – Vanji/Karur, port Muziris, emblem bow and arrow; Chola – Uraiyur, port Puhar (Kaveripattinam), emblem tiger; Pandya – Madurai, port Korkai, emblem fish.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Gupta Period (c. 320–550 CE) — the ‘Golden Age’ of north India; rulers Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II.

• Mauryan Period (322–185 BCE) — Chandragupta Maurya, Bindusara, Ashoka; capital Pataliputra.

• Mahajanapada period (c. 6th century BCE) — the 16 mahajanapadas of north India, with Magadha emerging supreme.

NOTE

• Sangam literature: Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettuthogai (eight anthologies), Pattuppattu (ten idylls), and the twin epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar).

• Famous Sangam-age Chera king Senguttuvan; Chola king Karikala (battle of Venni, built the Kallanai dam on the Kaveri).

question: Which among the following was set up in 1956 by Indian government by nationalising all the existing private sector life insurance companies?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Life Insurance Corporation of India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) was created on 1 September 1956 under the LIC Act, 1956, by nationalising 245 Indian and foreign life insurers and provident societies. (भारतीय जीवन बीमा निगम)

• Its headquarters is at Mumbai; its motto is ‘Yogakshemam Vahamyaham’ (Your welfare is our responsibility), taken from the Bhagavad Gita.

• LIC’s IPO in May 2022 was the largest ever in India; it remains majority-owned by the Government of India.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC) was formed in 1972 under the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, and began operations in 1973; it is today India’s national reinsurer.

• New India Assurance Company Limited (founded 1919 by Sir Dorabji Tata) and United India Insurance Company Limited (1938) are general (non-life) insurers that became GIC subsidiaries after 1972.

NOTE

• The insurance regulator is IRDAI, set up in 1999 (statutory in 2000), headquartered at Hyderabad.

• The four public-sector general insurers: New India Assurance, National Insurance, Oriental Insurance and United India Insurance.

question: The ‘Golden quadrilateral’ does not connect which of the following cities?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bhopal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Golden Quadrilateral (GQ) is a network of four/six-lane express highways connecting Delhi – Kolkata – Chennai – Mumbai – Delhi. Bhopal is not on this quadrilateral. (स्वर्णिम चतुर्भुज)

• Its total length is about 5,846 km and it is the largest project of the National Highways Development Project (NHDP), implemented by the NHAI (set up 1988, operational 1995).

• The project was launched under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee and was substantially completed in 2012.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Delhi–Kolkata and Delhi–Mumbai legs form the northern arms; Mumbai–Chennai and Chennai–Kolkata form the southern arms.

• The North–South Corridor runs Srinagar to Kanyakumari (about 4,000 km) and the East–West Corridor runs Silchar to Porbandar (about 3,300 km); these two corridors intersect at Jhansi.

NOTE

• NH-44 (Srinagar–Kanyakumari) is the longest national highway in India, about 3,745 km.

• Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017) is the current umbrella highway-development programme of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.

question: Azhar (2016), a sports-related movie, is based on which of the following sports?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cricket.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• ‘Azhar’ (2016) is a biographical sports film on the cricketer Mohammad Azharuddin, former captain of the Indian cricket team. (क्रिकेट)

• It was directed by Tony D’Souza, with Emraan Hashmi playing Azharuddin.

• Mohammad Azharuddin (born 1963, Hyderabad) scored centuries in his first three Test matches — a world record — and captained India in 47 Tests.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Mixed Martial Arts / wrestling — Dangal (2016) on the Phogat sisters and Mahavir Singh Phogat; Sultan (2016).

• Boxing — Mary Kom (2014) starring Priyanka Chopra; Toofaan (2021).

• Hockey — Chak De! India (2007) and Gold (2018), both starring Shah Rukh Khan and Akshay Kumar respectively.

NOTE

• Other cricket films: Lagaan (2001), M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story (2016), 83 (2021), Shabaash Mithu (2022), Jersey (2022).

• Athletics biopics: Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013) on Milkha Singh and Rashmi Rocket (2021).

question: Who among the following is a sitar maestro of global acclaim?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shahid Parvez Khan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ustad Shahid Parvez Khan (born 1955) is an internationally acclaimed sitar player of the Etawah (Imdadkhani) gharana. (सितार वादक)

• He is a seventh-generation musician of his family and was awarded the Padma Shri (2006) and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award (2007).

• The sitar is a plucked string instrument (tat vadya) associated with Hindustani classical music.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Ustad Bismillah Khan — legendary shehnai player; Bharat Ratna (2001); played at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947.

• Girija Devi — celebrated thumri vocalist of the Banaras (Seniya) gharana, known as ‘Appaji’; Padma Vibhushan (2016).

• Pandit Vishwa Mohan Bhatt — inventor and player of the Mohan Veena (modified slide guitar); Grammy Award (1994) for ‘A Meeting by the River’ with Ry Cooder.

NOTE

• Other sitar exponents: Pandit Ravi Shankar (Bharat Ratna 1999), Ustad Vilayat Khan, Nikhil Banerjee, Anoushka Shankar.

• Instrument–artist pairs: Sarod – Amjad Ali Khan, Santoor – Shivkumar Sharma, Flute – Hariprasad Chaurasia, Tabla – Zakir Hussain, Sarangi – Ram Narayan.

question: In which Indian movement, were the issues faced by indigo planters, first brought to light in 1917?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Champaran Satyagraha.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Champaran Satyagraha (1917) in Bihar was Mahatma Gandhi’s first satyagraha in India, launched on behalf of indigo cultivators exploited by European planters. (चंपारन सत्याग्रह)

• Peasants were forced under the tinkathia system to grow indigo on 3/20th of their holding; Gandhi was invited by the local cultivator Raj Kumar Shukla.

• Gandhi’s enquiry led to the Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918, which abolished the tinkathia system. Associates included Rajendra Prasad, J.B. Kripalani, Brajkishore Prasad and Mazharul Haque.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Kheda Satyagraha (1918, Gujarat) — a no-revenue campaign for peasants after crop failure; Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel rose to prominence here.

• Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) — Gandhi’s first hunger strike, for a wage hike for textile mill workers; Anasuya Sarabhai supported it.

• Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) — a nationwide movement withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922).

NOTE

• Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915; his political mentor was Gopal Krishna Gokhale.

• Earlier indigo protest: the Indigo Revolt (Nil Vidroha) of 1859–60 in Bengal, depicted in Dinabandhu Mitra’s play ‘Nil Darpan’.

question: ______ are the vessels which carry carbon dioxide-rich blood back to the heart.
solution_text:
The correct answer is veins.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Veins carry deoxygenated (carbon dioxide-rich) blood from the body back to the heart; they have thin walls and valves that prevent the backflow of blood. (शिराएँ)

• The superior and inferior vena cava bring deoxygenated blood into the right atrium of the heart.

• Exception: the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Arteries carry blood away from the heart; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls and no valves. Exception: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

• Capillaries are the thinnest blood vessels (one-cell-thick walls) where exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes takes place between blood and tissues.

• Neurons are nerve cells, not blood vessels; they transmit electrical impulses.

NOTE

• The aorta is the largest artery; the vena cava is the largest vein in the human body.

• Human blood circulation is double circulation — pulmonary and systemic; it was discovered by William Harvey.

question: The Narmada river rises in the Amarkantak hills situated in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madhya Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Narmada rises from the Amarkantak plateau in Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh, at a height of about 1,057 m. (नर्मदा — अमरकंटक, मध्य प्रदेश)

• It is the longest west-flowing river of India (about 1,312 km) and flows through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges before entering the Gulf of Khambhat (Arabian Sea).

• It forms the Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur, where it cuts through the Marble Rocks (Bhedaghat).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Narmada flows through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat; the Sardar Sarovar Dam is in Gujarat.

• The Statue of Unity (Sardar Patel, world’s tallest statue, 182 m, unveiled 2018) stands on the Narmada at Kevadia, Gujarat.

• Rajasthan has the Chambal, Banas and Luni; the Luni is a west-flowing river that ends in the Rann of Kachchh.

NOTE

• Other west-flowing peninsular rivers: Tapi (Multai, MP), Mahi, Sabarmati, Periyar, Sharavati.

• Amarkantak is also the source of the Son river (a Ganga tributary) and the Johila.

question: The first urban settlement to reach a population of one million was ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is London.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• London was the first urban settlement in the world to cross a population of one million, achieving that status around 1810 (standard NCERT figure). (लंदन — प्रथम मिलियन नगर)

• Its rapid growth was driven by the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the mid-18th century and pulled rural populations into the cities.

• A city with a population of over one million is called a million city; by 1982 there were about 175 such cities in the world.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Paris became a million city in 1850 and New York in 1860 — both after London.

• Tokyo is today the world’s largest urban agglomeration by population, but it reached the million mark much later than London.

• Berlin grew as an industrial capital in the later 19th century.

NOTE

• A megacity has a population of over 10 million; India’s megacities per Census 2011 include Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.

• Kolkata (Calcutta) was India’s first million city (around 1901).

question: Which of the following Indian state is biggest in terms of area?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rajasthan is the largest Indian state by area, covering about 3,42,239 sq km, roughly 10.4% of India’s total area. (राजस्थान — क्षेत्रफल में सबसे बड़ा)

• Capital: Jaipur; it shares an international border with Pakistan (the Radcliffe Line) and contains the Thar Desert and the Aravalli range, India’s oldest fold mountains.

• Order of the largest states by area: Rajasthan > Madhya Pradesh > Maharashtra > Uttar Pradesh > Gujarat.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Madhya Pradesh (about 3,08,245 sq km) is the second largest; it was the largest before the creation of Chhattisgarh in 2000.

• Maharashtra (about 3,07,713 sq km) is third; Uttar Pradesh (about 2,40,928 sq km) is fourth by area but first in population.

NOTE

• Goa is the smallest state by area; Sikkim is the smallest by population.

• Ladakh is the largest Union Territory by area; Lakshadweep is the smallest UT by area.

• Highest peak of the Aravallis: Guru Shikhar (Mount Abu, 1,722 m).

question: Kathakali dance form originated from which of the following states?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kerala.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kathakali is a classical dance-drama of Kerala, developed in about the 17th century; the word means ‘story-play’ (katha = story, kali = play). (कथकली — केरल)

• It is famous for elaborate chutti (face) make-up, huge headgear and colour-coded characters — Pacha (green, noble), Kathi (anti-hero), Thadi (bearded), Kari (black) and Minukku.

• Themes come mostly from the Ramayana and Mahabharata; it is traditionally performed by men. Exponents: Kalamandalam Ramankutty Nair, Kalamandalam Gopi, Guru Kunchu Kurup.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Tamil Nadu — Bharatanatyam, the oldest classical dance, based on the Natya Shastra; exponents Rukmini Devi Arundale, Balasaraswati.

• Odisha — Odissi, associated with the Jagannath temple and the Mahari tradition; exponents Kelucharan Mohapatra, Sonal Mansingh.

• Karnataka — Yakshagana, a folk theatre form (Kathakali is not from Karnataka).

NOTE

• The eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam (TN), Kathak (UP), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Mohiniyattam is the other classical dance of Kerala, performed solo by women in white-and-gold kasavu attire.

question: The objects which repeats its motion after some time is called ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is periodic motion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Periodic motion is motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time; that interval is called the time period (T). (आवर्त गति)

• Examples: the swing of a simple pendulum, the hands of a clock, the vibration of a tuning fork, the revolution of the Earth around the Sun.

• Frequency (f) is the number of repetitions per second and is the reciprocal of the time period: f = 1/T, measured in hertz (Hz).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Rectilinear motion — motion along a straight line, e.g., a car on a straight road or a freely falling body.

• Circular motion — motion along a circular path, e.g., a stone whirled on a string; it is periodic only if it is uniform and completed repeatedly.

• Semi-circular motion is simply motion along half a circle and does not by itself imply repetition.

NOTE

• Oscillatory motion is a periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position, e.g., a pendulum or a loaded spring; every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory.

• Time period of a simple pendulum: T = 2π√(l/g) — it depends on length and gravity, not on the mass of the bob.

question: Who among the following is not associated with Kuchipudi dance form?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ghanakanta Bora Borbayan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ghanakanta Bora Borbayan is an exponent of Sattriya, the classical dance of Assam, not of Kuchipudi; he received the Padma Shri (2020). (सत्रिया — असम)

• Kuchipudi is the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh, named after the village Kuchelapuram in Krishna district; it was systematised by Siddhendra Yogi (Bhama Kalapam).

• A signature Kuchipudi item is the Tarangam, in which the dancer performs balancing on the rim of a brass plate, often with a pot of water on the head.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Vempati Chinna Satyam — the doyen of modern Kuchipudi, founder of the Kuchipudi Art Academy, Chennai; Padma Bhushan (1998).

• Vyjayanthi Kashi — a leading Kuchipudi dancer and choreographer based in Bengaluru.

• Radha Reddy — of the celebrated Raja and Radha Reddy duo, Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan awardees in Kuchipudi.

NOTE

• Sattriya was founded by the Vaishnava saint Srimanta Sankaradeva in 15th-century Assam and was recognised as a classical dance by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000.

• Other Kuchipudi names: Yamini Krishnamurthy, Swapnasundari, Shobha Naidu.

question: भारतीय संविधान के 42वें संशोधन की प्रस्तावना में निम्नलिखित में से कौन-से शब्द जोड़े गए थे?
solution_text:
The correct answer is समाजवादी (Socialist).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 added three words to the Preamble — समाजवादी (Socialist), पंथनिरपेक्ष (Secular) and अखंडता (Integrity). (42वाँ संशोधन, 1976)

• The Preamble thus changed from ‘Sovereign Democratic Republic’ to ‘Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic’, and ‘unity of the Nation’ became ‘unity and integrity of the Nation’.

• The 42nd Amendment, passed during the Emergency (1975–77) under Indira Gandhi, is called the ‘Mini-Constitution’; it was based on the Swaran Singh Committee recommendations.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• सार्वभौम (Sovereign), लोकतांत्रिक (Democratic) and गणतंत्र (Republic) were part of the original Preamble adopted on 26 November 1949.

• The 42nd Amendment also added Part IVA – Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and the words ‘education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife’ to the Concurrent List.

NOTE

• The Preamble has been amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment.

• In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held the Preamble to be a part of the Constitution and amendable, subject to the basic structure doctrine.

• The 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many 42nd Amendment provisions and removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights (Article 300A).

question: Which among the following bills passed in Parliament in 2022 replaced the Identification of Prisoners Act, 1920?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Bill.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 replaced the century-old Identification of Prisoners Act, 1920. (दंड प्रक्रिया (शिनाख्त) अधिनियम, 2022)

• It authorises the police and prison authorities to collect ‘measurements’ of convicts and arrested persons — finger and palm prints, footprints, photographs, iris and retina scans, physical and biological samples and behavioural attributes.

• The National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) is empowered to store and share such records, which may be retained for 75 years. It was introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs and received presidential assent in April 2022.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 allowed the linking of the electoral roll with Aadhaar (voluntarily) and provided four qualifying dates for enrolment.

• The Farm Laws Repeal Act, 2021 repealed the three farm laws of 2020 after the farmers’ agitation.

• The Central Vigilance Commission (Amendment) Act, 2021 extended the tenure of the CBI and ED Directors up to a maximum of five years.

NOTE

• The 1920 Act allowed only fingerprints, footprints and photographs, and only of a limited class of convicts — the 2022 Act greatly widened both the data and the persons covered.

• The NCRB was set up in 1986 and functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

question: किस भारतीय मंत्रालय ने जम्मू और कश्मीर पुनर्गठन विधेयक, 2019 पेश किया था?
solution_text:
The correct answer is गृह मंत्रालय (Ministry of Home Affairs).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Bill, 2019 was introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs; Home Minister Amit Shah moved it in the Rajya Sabha on 5 August 2019. (गृह मंत्रालय)

• The Act bifurcated the State of Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories — Jammu and Kashmir (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without a legislature) — with effect from 31 October 2019.

• On the same day the special status under Article 370 was made inoperative by a Presidential Order, and Article 35A ceased to apply.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Ministry of Home Affairs handles internal security, Centre–State relations, border management, disaster management and UT administration.

• The Ministry of Defence deals with the armed forces; the Ministry of External Affairs with foreign relations; the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs with legislative business coordination.

NOTE

• 31 October is observed as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day), the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

• India now has 28 states and 8 Union Territories; Ladakh’s capitals are Leh and Kargil.

• In In Re Article 370 (December 2023) the Supreme Court upheld the abrogation and directed restoration of statehood to J&K.
